story.title: Former Kosovo President Thaci Convicted of War Crimes and Sentenced to 25 Years
story.summary: Hashim Thaci, the former President of Kosovo, has been convicted of war crimes by a tribunal in The Hague and sentenced to 25 years in prison. The court found him guilty of crimes committed during Kosovo's war for independence from Serbia, including murder, torture, and illegal arrests. The verdict has elicited strong reactions among the people of Kosovo.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a conviction?
explore_lenses.title: A six-year case centered on KLA leadership
explore_lenses.summary: The case grew from a 2020 indictment against four former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders and a trial that began in April 2023. The panel ultimately distinguished between the defendants’ individual responsibility and the broader legitimacy of Kosovo’s independence struggle.

claims.text: The operative indictment alleged crimes from March 1998 through September 1999 in Kosovo and northern Albania, and charged Thaçi and three co-defendants with six crimes-against-humanity counts and four war-crimes counts.
The trial began on April 3, 2023; proceedings closed in December 2025 after 134 witnesses testified, and closing statements were held in February 2026.

The panel convicted Thaçi of four war-crimes counts—arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder—while acquitting all four defendants of the crimes-against-humanity counts because prosecutors did not prove a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.

Thaçi maintained that he was innocent and sought a full acquittal; prosecutors argued the evidence showed the defendants targeted political opponents and people perceived as collaborators or traitors.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this verdict matter in Kosovo?
explore_lenses.title: It tests accountability amid a contested war legacy
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling concerns crimes attributed to senior KLA leaders, who remain widely regarded by many Kosovars as figures of the independence struggle. It has therefore produced both a judicial-accountability narrative and strong claims that the court misreads Kosovo’s wartime history.

claims.text: The judgment found that 385 people were arbitrarily detained, 49 cruelly treated, 303 tortured and 96 murdered; the court said the victims included political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators.
Presiding Judge Charles Smith said the case was not about the legitimacy of the KLA or its objective of Kosovo’s independence, but about personal criminal responsibility.

Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca called the verdict a terrible judgment for Kosovo, its people and its liberation war; before the ruling, demonstrators and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama had also portrayed the proceedings as an attack on the liberation narrative.
Specialist Prosecutor Kimberly West said the decision showed that individuals who exploited wartime conditions to commit grave crimes were being held accountable.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the 25-year sentence?
explore_lenses.title: Appeals and a separate pending case remain
explore_lenses.summary: The 25-year sentence is subject to appeal, so it is not necessarily the final outcome. Thaçi also remains a defendant in a distinct Kosovo Specialist Chambers case concerning alleged offenses against the administration of justice.

story_report.summary: A Hague-based Kosovo tribunal convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi of war crimes committed during the 1998-99 conflict and sentenced him to 25 years in prison. The panel found him guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, while acquitting the defendants of crimes against humanity after finding prosecutors had not proved a widespread and systematic attack on civilians. Thaçi, who has maintained his innocence, may appeal the judgment; prosecutors may also challenge the outcome.

sections.heading: Charges Spanned Kosovo and Northern Albania
sections.body: The indictment alleged crimes committed from March 1998 through September 1999 in Kosovo and northern Albania. Thaçi and three co-defendants faced six counts of crimes against humanity and four war-crimes counts. The trial opened in April 2023 and closed in December 2025 after testimony from 134 witnesses; closing arguments followed in February 2026.

sections.heading: Judgment Addressed Individual Criminal Responsibility
sections.body: The court found that 385 people were arbitrarily detained, 49 were cruelly treated, 303 were tortured and 96 were murdered. It said victims included political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators. Presiding Judge Charles Smith said the case concerned individual criminal responsibility rather than the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army or its aim of achieving Kosovo’s independence.

sections.heading: Kosovo Leaders Contest the Verdict
sections.body: Reactions in Kosovo were mixed. Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca called the ruling a terrible judgment for Kosovo, its people and its liberation war; demonstrators and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama had similarly characterized the proceedings as an attack on the liberation narrative. Specialist Prosecutor Kimberly West said the decision held to account people who exploited wartime conditions to commit grave crimes.

unresolved.text: The sources consulted did not include the full written judgment and its detailed factual and legal findings.
No appeal timetable or appellate outcome has been established, and no date is available for a judgment in Thaçi’s separate administration-of-justice case.
The longer-term effects on Kosovo’s domestic politics and relations with Serbia cannot be determined from immediate reactions.

related_stories.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte made his first appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. The 81-year-old is facing accusations of crimes against humanity, with discussions regarding his health and memory impairment taking place during the session.

related_stories.title: Saudi Arabia Claims Houthi Drone Targeted Mecca, Warns of Consequences
related_stories.summary: Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen's Houthi rebels of attempting to attack Mecca, Islam's holiest city, claiming its air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone deployed by the Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition emphasized that the security of Mecca is a 'red line' and warned of potential deterrent measures. In response, the Houthis have denied the allegations, labeling them as false.

related_stories.title: Escalating Conflict: Houthis Claim Downing Saudi Jet, Saudis Accuse of Drone Attack Near Mecca
related_stories.summary: The Houthi militia in Yemen has claimed to have downed a Saudi jet, while the Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of launching a drone attack near Mecca, which the Houthis denied. This exchange of accusations marks a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict, with the Houthis also threatening Saudi oil exports by seizing parts of Yemen's Red Sea.

related_stories.title: House Panel Holds Leon Black in Contempt Over Epstein Investigation
related_stories.summary: The House Oversight Committee voted to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt for failing to comply with subpoenas related to its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. Survivors of Epstein have expressed support for the committee's decision and are urging for prosecution against Black following his contempt conviction.
